author: nflaig
content: there is an issue on each EL repo for this already

author: nflaig
content: but there was a question from Erigon on why this is needed, explained here https://github.com/erigontech/erigon/issues/24100#issuecomment-5908405242

author: nero_eth
content: At a 200M gas limit with BALs growing linearly from today's measured ~72 KiB (about 241 KiB compressed per block), retaining BALs for 3,533 epochs is about 28 GB. Retaining for 14,299 epochs is 113 GB, so this adds 85 GB of compressed BAL data per node (130 GB uncompressed).

author: nflaig
content: we can probably reduce this to 8192 with Kev's EIP https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8383 in hegota

author: nflaig
content:
other than that, to decouple this dependency further we would need
- https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8146 (so bals are no longer part of `ExecutionPayload`)
- or https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8237 (which completely removes the payload syncing on CL side)

author: nflaig
content: but what Marius is saying here https://discord.com/channels/595666850260713488/1551749131289235487, it seems BALs help out a lot during full sync for ELs as well

author: nero_eth
content:
yes they do.
ELs that are offline for longer than 3533 epochs, are maybe better-off re-syncing using snap than trying to catch up, but this is still to be validated.
Without a BAL they have a 4-8x disadvantage compared to nodes at the tip of the chain. They can use the full slot (12s) vs only 6s of it (= worst-case at tip of the chain), so they also get a 2x.
Still, they end up 2-4x slower (which for avg blocks is still easily doable as we don't see blocks that take that long to execute),  so they would probably still easily catch up, but longer retention would def help here

author: tersec
content: Looks like 8146 was already DFI'd also

author: nero_eth
content:
Correcting myself, I don't think that discarding state and starting with a fresh snap sync is fast for avg node setups. There's just a lot of state to download for mainnet.
So, keeping more BALs is not only great for CL blinding - avoiding keeping duplicated data on both layers, and also for EL catch-up with re-execution.

author: nflaig
content: yeah both of these are DFI'd, just floating ideas how we can remove this dependency, but if BALs are required for efficient full sync this might not be a good idea either way

author: jochembrouwer
content:
Can we find out in ELs that if we are beyond BAL retention window that we do not discard old state, but use BALs (of those what we can retrieve, so at least ~3533) to help with healing? This seems like snap/1 healing phase, but we get bonus that all recent "touches" are in the BAL (which helps sync with snap/2)
Maybe <@402853454126776320> has some ideas here? 😄

author: nero_eth
content:
it's a trade off, after all. 
I'd say it's more "in theory" they are useful for full-sync catch-up. In practice nodes are rarely offline for that long and would probably accept re-sync. In the end we increase disk footprint for every node such that a tiny fraction can catch up faster.

author: nero_eth
content: healing is not the problem here, syncing on the EL neither. It's more that CL nodes want to blind the BALs but can't because in order to provide valid responses to peer they would also need to unblind the BALs again and, right now, only geth would be a reliable partner to do so because they for sure still have the BAL.

author: nero_eth
content: To me it sounds reasonable to extend the retention window to 14299 * 32 blocks, and as a follow-up, we should integrate the non-finality clause for keeping more BALs in cases of non-finality (which might be a more involved change)
